extracted_claims.text: Under the AI Act, providers of general-purpose AI (GPAI) models must maintain technical documentation, make it available to authorities and downstream providers, establish a copyright policy, and publish a summary of training data (Article 53).
Open-source GPAI models are exempt from some documentation requirements unless they are classified as having systemic risk.

Providers of GPAI models with systemic risk have additional obligations under Article 55, including performing model evaluations, assessing and mitigating systemic risks, tracking and reporting serious incidents, and ensuring adequate cybersecurity protection.
A GPAI model is presumed to pose systemic risk if it is trained using cumulative compute exceeding 10^25 floating-point operations (FLOPs), per Article 51.

The Commission can also designate a model as posing systemic risk via a decision (ex officio or following a qualified alert from the scientific panel) based on Annex XIII criteria, even absent meeting the compute threshold.
The EU AI Act entered into force on 1 August 2024.
GPAI obligations under the AI Act apply to providers placing models on the market from 2 August 2025 onwards.
Enforcement powers for GPAI obligations arrived in 2026, with older models given a transition period.

The General-Purpose AI Code of Practice is a voluntary tool that signatories can use to demonstrate compliance with AI Act obligations, particularly for GPAI models with systemic risk (the Safety and Security Chapter).

Providers of GPAI models with systemic risk must notify the AI Office without delay and, if signatories to the Code, confirm their risk-management Framework within four weeks of notifying the Commission and at least two weeks before market launch.

Major GPAI providers including Amazon, Anthropic, Google, IBM, Microsoft, Mistral AI, and OpenAI signed the Code of Practice; xAI signed only the Safety and Security chapter; Meta declined to sign the Code.
Providers that do not sign the Code of Practice must demonstrate compliance with AI Act obligations through other adequate means.

President Biden signed Executive Order 14110, 'Safe, Secure, and Trustworthy Development and Use of Artificial Intelligence,' on October 30, 2023, directing executive agencies to take various AI-related actions, including labeling/authentication guidance and reporting requirements with specific deadlines.
President Trump revoked Biden's AI Executive Order 14110 upon taking office in January 2025.

On January 23, 2025, President Trump issued an executive order titled 'Removing Barriers to American Leadership in Artificial Intelligence,' directing advisers to coordinate development of an AI action plan.
Following the Biden EO's revocation, replacement federal AI policies had not yet been drafted as of early 2025.

On July 23, 2025, the Trump Administration released America's AI Action Plan, outlining more than 90 federal policy actions across three pillars: Accelerating Innovation, Building American AI Infrastructure, and Leading in International Diplomacy and Security.

The AI Action Plan and related executive orders emphasize deregulation, infrastructure expansion (energy, data centers, semiconductors), and US global AI leadership rather than imposing binding safety obligations on foundation model developers akin to the EU's systemic-risk regime.
Executive Order 14318, 'Accelerating Federal Permitting of Data Center Infrastructure,' directs agencies to expedite permitting for large AI data centers (over 100 MW) and related infrastructure.
President Trump signed Executive Order 14362 on November 24, 2025, launching the 'Genesis Mission,' a national effort to build an integrated AI platform for scientific discovery.

On December 11, 2025, President Trump signed an Executive Order titled 'Ensuring a National Policy Framework for Artificial Intelligence,' aiming to establish a uniform, minimally burdensome federal AI standard and to preempt the patchwork of state AI laws, with limited exceptions (e.g., child safety protections).

The December 2025 EO directs development of a federal legislative recommendation to preempt state AI laws rather than itself enacting binding substantive AI safety requirements for foundation model providers.

As of late 2025, the US federal approach to AI has consisted primarily of executive orders promoting innovation, infrastructure, and deregulation, with no enacted federal statute imposing EU-style systemic-risk obligations (e.g., mandatory risk assessments, incident reporting, cybersecurity requirements) on foundation model developers.

# EU AI Act vs. US Federal AI Policy: Comparing Approaches to Foundation Model Governance

## Executive Summary
The EU AI Act imposes binding, tiered legal obligations on general-purpose AI (GPAI) model providers, with heightened requirements for models posing "systemic risk," while US federal policy has relied almost entirely on executive orders favoring deregulation, infrastructure expansion, and state-law preemption rather than binding safety mandates. As of late 2025, no enacted US federal statute imposes obligations comparable to the EU's systemic-risk regime (medium confidence).

## Key Findings

### EU AI Act: Binding Obligations for GPAI Providers
Under Article 53, GPAI providers must maintain technical documentation, share it with authorities and downstream providers, establish a copyright policy, and publish a training-data summary (medium confidence) ([AI Act Service Desk](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/article-53)). Open-source models are exempt from some of these requirements unless classified as posing systemic risk (medium confidence) ([AI Act Service Desk](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/article-53)). Providers of GPAI models with systemic risk face additional Article 55 duties: model evaluations, systemic risk assessment and mitigation, serious-incident tracking/reporting, and cybersecurity protections (medium confidence) ([Digital Strategy FAQ](https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/faqs/general-purpose-ai-models-ai-act-questions-answers)). A model is presumed systemic-risk if trained with cumulative compute exceeding 10^25 FLOPs under Article 51 (high confidence) ([AI Act Service Desk](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/article-51)), and the Commission can also designate systemic-risk status via Annex XIII criteria absent meeting this threshold (medium confidence) ([AI Act Service Desk](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/article-51)).

### EU Implementation Timeline and Voluntary Compliance Tools
The Act entered into force 1 August 2024 (medium confidence) ([JRC](https://publications.jrc.ec.europa.eu/repository/bitstream/JRC143260/JRC143260_01.pdf)), with GPAI obligations applying from 2 August 2025 (high confidence) ([Digital Strategy FAQ](https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/faqs/questions-and-answers-code-practice-general-purpose-ai)). The voluntary General-Purpose AI Code of Practice lets signatories demonstrate compliance, particularly via its Safety and Security Chapter for systemic-risk models (medium confidence) ([Code of Practice](https://artificialintelligenceact.eu/introduction-to-code-of-practice)). Systemic-risk providers must notify the AI Office without delay, and Code signatories must confirm risk-management frameworks within set deadlines (high confidence) ([Digital Strategy FAQ](https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/faqs/questions-and-answers-code-practice-general-purpose-ai)). Major providers including Amazon, Anthropic, Google, IBM, Microsoft, Mistral AI, and OpenAI signed the Code; Meta declined (low confidence) ([Founderz](https://founderz.com/blog/what-is-gpai-model)).

### US Federal Approach: Executive Orders, Deregulation, Preemption
Biden's Executive Order 14110 (October 2023) directed agencies toward labeling, authentication guidance, and reporting deadlines (high confidence) ([Federal Register](https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2023/11/01/2023-24283/safe-secure-and-trustworthy-development-and-use-of-artificial-intelligence)), but Trump revoked it upon taking office in January 2025 (medium confidence) ([Wiley](https://www.wiley.law/alert-President-Trump-Revokes-Biden-Administrations-AI-EO-What-To-Know)), replacing it with an order prioritizing "American AI leadership" (medium confidence) ([Squire Patton Boggs](https://www.squirepattonboggs.com/insights/publications/key-insights-on-president-trumps-new-ai-executive-order-and-policy-regulatory-implications)). Replacement policies were not yet drafted in early 2025 (medium confidence) ([Skadden](https://www.skadden.com/insights/publications/executive-briefing/ai-broad-biden-order-is-withdrawn)). In July 2025, the Administration released America's AI Action Plan, with 90+ actions emphasizing innovation, infrastructure, and global leadership rather than binding safety obligations (medium confidence) ([Sidley](https://www.sidley.com/en/insights/newsupdates/2025/07/the-trump-administrations-2025-ai-action-plan)). In December 2025, an executive order sought a uniform federal AI standard preempting state laws, directing development of a legislative recommendation rather than enacting binding substantive requirements itself (medium confidence) ([MVA Law](https://www.mvalaw.com/data-points/president-trump-takes-aim-at-state-artificial-intelligence-regulation-with-limited-exceptions)).

## Contradictions & Uncertainties
Sources disagree on whether current models exceed the EU's 10^25 FLOPs threshold or merely approach it, likely due to differing publication dates ([European Parliament item](https://ec.europa.eu/newsroom/eismea/redirection/item/825283/en/3098) vs. [EDPB, June 2025](https://www.edpb.europa.eu/system/files/2025-06/spe-training-on-ai-and-data-protection-legal_en.pdf)). The exact sequencing of Trump's EO revocation and replacement order is unclear across sources. Low-confidence claims include enforcement timing for GPAI obligations arriving in 2026 ([Founderz](https://founderz.com/blog/what-is-gpai-model)), details of Code of Practice signatories ([LinkedIn post](https://www.linkedin.com/posts/joel-kaplan-63905618_europe-is-heading-down-the-wrong-path-on-activity-7351928745668055042-XuF7)), and the Genesis Mission EO ([Portland State](https://web.pdx.edu/~pcooper/TechLawPolicy-css.html)).

## Knowledge Gaps
No source confirms whether the US plans any binding federal statute comparable to the EU's Article 51/55 regime. The content and legislative prospects of the federal preemption recommendation remain unspecified. Practical enforcement of EU GPAI obligations since 2026, Meta's compliance status absent Code signature, and interactions between US federal initiatives and existing frameworks (e.g., NIST) are unaddressed. Cross-jurisdictional reconciliation for companies subject to both regimes is also unexplored.
